content.p: On 21 November 1894 Japanese troops took the Chinese naval fortress of Port Arthur, today called Lüshun, in a single day. What followed has been argued over for more than a century. Foreign correspondents who had marched in with the Japanese Second Army said that soldiers spent days killing prisoners and townspeople. The Japanese foreign minister conceded that the troops had broken all restraints, promised an investigation and protested against exaggeration, while officials claimed that townspeople had fired from the houses. One history site says no senior Japanese officer faced charges or public punishment.

The number of dead is still disputed. Estimates in the sources used here run from about 2,000 to 4,500 on one side, up to a figure of 20,000 that foreign journalists were said to have reported early on. Nobody is recorded as having counted the bodies, and one eyewitness wrote that he could not.
content.h2: A fortress built to be impregnable
content.p: Port Arthur was the Qing empire's showpiece naval base. According to a war history reprinted on sinojapanesewar.com, the authorities decided in 1881 to build a dockyard there. Native contractors proved unequal to the task, and in 1887 a French company took over and finished the work in three years. The result was a large basin, two dry docks, foundries and workshops, a harbour that stayed free of ice in winter, and forts armed with heavy Krupp guns whose gunners had been trained by a German officer, Constantin von Hanneken. The same account puts the town's population at about six thousand, not counting the garrison, and says it had two large temples, two theatres and several banks.

The base sat at the end of a narrow peninsula. To reach it the Japanese first had to take the walled city of Jinzhou and the forts guarding Dalian Bay. The Second Army, under Field Marshal Ōyama Iwao, landed on the Liaodong Peninsula in the autumn. James Creelman, who was travelling with it for Joseph Pulitzer's New York World, later wrote that the army took Jinzhou after an artillery duel of about an hour and that the Japanese then took the seven forts around Dalian Bay, one group of which the Chinese had abandoned during the night. At Jinzhou, he said, a few women, children and old men had been killed by shellfire, and the terrified inhabitants were on their knees to their conquerors.

By then the Japanese had won a run of victories, including Pyongyang in September and Jiuliancheng in October. The History Skills site says the 1st Division of General Yamaji Motoharu led the advance on Port Arthur and had orders to wipe out resistance. The same page adds that no written order authorising a massacre has been found. Britannica's account of the war sets the scene: by March 1895 the Japanese held Manchuria and part of Shandong, and China was suing for peace.

The war history on sinojapanesewar.com says the Japanese infantry entered the town from about two in the afternoon on the 21st, and that the regiment sent against the principal coast fort, on Golden Hill, passed through the streets and took the hill without much difficulty. The Chinese abandoned the remaining forts overnight. The writer concluded that the fortress had in effect fallen in a single day, and blamed the Chinese for relying on guns while neglecting trained infantry. Japan's own archives hold the paperwork of the assault. The Japan Center for Asian Historical Records lists a detailed battle report by Colonel Wada Yūkyū of the Second Army's siege park, sent to Ōyama, and Ōyama's administrative regulations for the captured port, sent to the General Staff on 4 December.

The History Skills page says resistance was weak because Qing command had collapsed after earlier defeats, and that defenders either abandoned their posts or surrendered. It says soldiers then began killing Chinese prisoners, some of them already disarmed, and that the killing spread to civilians as troops went house to house looking for hidden soldiers.

The fullest eyewitness account in the sources opened here is quoted, without a name attached, on the sinojapanesewar.com page as the report of a "western observer". He says he watched from a hill called White Boulders, which gave him a close view of the whole town, together with the British and American military attachés. He swore that he saw "practically every shot fired" and that "not one came from any but Japanese". He described men who knelt and bowed their heads to the ground in submission before being killed, and a horseman who rode into a creek and slashed an old man and two children, aged ten and twelve, a dozen times with his sword.

The same witness says the killing did not stop with the battle. "Thursday, Friday, Saturday, and Sunday were spent by the soldiery in murder and pillage from dawn to dark," he writes, adding that men's bodies lay in the streets "in hundreds, perhaps thousands, for we could not count". He says he saw groups of prisoners tied together, shot, and then hacked. He puts the fighting dead at no more than one hundred and says that "at least two thousand unarmed men were put to death". He saw a Reuters correspondent, Mr. Hart, robbed of everything but his clothes, and says Hart's cook and two kitchen boys were shot at their stove. Meanwhile, he says, the field marshal and his officers listened to a military band and a roar of "Banzai Nippon" from twenty thousand throats.

Japanese officials claimed that townspeople had been armed and had fired from the houses. The observer says he found cartridges of the type described but "never saw one fired", and never saw an attack from a house. He did not hide a possible cause of the rage. He wrote that Japanese soldiers captured earlier had been found mutilated, with hands and heads cut off, and that placards offered rewards for heads, hands or prisoners. In his words, the Chinese had "committed nameless atrocities which the Japanese repaid a hundred fold". The compiler of the sinojapanesewar.com page likewise says the Japanese were infuriated after Chinese soldiers mutilated Japanese bodies and displayed them at the town entrance. The page puts the killing of the remaining population at between two and three thousand, without distinction of age or sex.

The same page names three correspondents who entered the town with the army: Creelman of the New York World, Frederic Villiers of the London Standard and Thomas Cowan of the Times. A different site gives Villiers as the source for a claim that only 36 residents survived. That figure comes from a LinkedIn essay marking the 123rd anniversary, and it also says the massacre lasted from 21 to 24 November and killed between 1,000 and 20,000 people.

Journalists could file their reports only after leaving the army's area, so the news was slow to arrive. Creelman's front-page dispatch ran in the New York World on 12 December, according to the Worldlymind history. It said the troops had "massacred practically the entire population in cold blood", that "the defenseless and unarmed inhabitants were butchered in their houses" and that the reign of murder "continued for three days". The sinojapanesewar.com compilation says other leading American newspapers denounced the story as false at first, and that a month later it was found to be true "in every essential particular".

The reaction in Tokyo is documented in the Worldlymind account. On 17 December the World printed a cable from the Foreign Minister, Mutsu Munemitsu, who conceded that the soldiers, "transported with rage at the mutilation of their comrades by the enemy", had "broke through all restraints" and inflicted vengeance without discrimination. Mutsu also protested against "exaggerations calculated to present the affair in a distorted and misleading aspect" and said there had been "absolutely no intention to harm or molest non-combatants". He promised an investigation.

Creelman wrote to his wife from Yokohama that he was "the general target for abuse in Japan simply because I have told the truth about Port Arthur". He said he had known that laying out the facts would set off "the vast enginery of abuse maintained by the Japanese government". Worldlymind adds that Japanese officials were reported to have accused Western reporters of feeding atrocity allegations to opposition papers, notably the English-language Yokohama Journal. The History Skills page says military censors limited coverage inside Japan, and that most Japanese newspapers ignored the reports while celebrating the capture.

History Skills states that no senior Japanese officer faced formal charges or public punishment and that no inquiry was launched to fix responsibility; it adds that no international legal mechanism then existed to investigate such crimes. That sits uneasily with Mutsu's promise of an investigation, and the sources opened here do not show what, if anything, came of it. The page records that a small number of Japanese writers and Buddhist leaders privately worried the massacre had stained the country's reputation. Among foreign diplomats, it says, trust in Japan's image as a civilised power declined somewhat.

Worldlymind argues the damage was brief. Admirers of Japan, it says, came to treat Port Arthur as an aberration, and Creelman himself, in his 1901 memoir, returned to a favourable view of Japan's conduct. The site's author, who is writing with hindsight, goes further and draws a line from the reporting to Japan's later wars, a connection that is his own argument rather than a finding of any court.

The war ended with the Treaty of Shimonoseki in April 1895. According to Britannica, China recognised Korea's independence and ceded Taiwan, the Pescadores and the Liaodong Peninsula, and agreed to pay a large indemnity. Russian, French and German pressure then forced Japan to give the Liaodong Peninsula back. History Skills says Russia promptly occupied and fortified Port Arthur, and that Japan retook it in 1905 in the Russo-Japanese War after a long siege. Worldlymind notes that the 1904 war opened with a Japanese surprise attack on the Russian squadron in the harbour.

The History Skills page says many Chinese historians have cited the 1894 killings as a warning of what Japanese aggression could bring, while Western critics saw them as a failure of military restraint. The LinkedIn essay notes that the Soviet Union withdrew its troops from Lüshun in May 1955.

Three questions are still open in the material available here. The first is the toll. History Skills gives later estimates of roughly 2,000 to 4,500 and early foreign press reports as high as 20,000. The sinojapanesewar.com compilation says between two and three thousand were killed. The LinkedIn essay gives a range of 1,000 to 20,000, and Worldlymind quotes Creelman's report that practically the entire population was massacred. The second is provocation: the mutilation of Japanese dead is reported by an eyewitness, but his judgment was that it did not justify what he saw. The third is responsibility, because no order has been found and no one was tried.
